claims.text: The studied material is homogeneous, single-phase, Co-free solidified FeNiCrMn without secondary phases or cast defects.
Dynamic mechanical behavior in single-phase solidified FeNiCrMn is governed by a shift between thermally activated dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Dislocation glide dominates FeNiCrMn deformation at room temperature and moderate strain rates.
Lower temperatures and higher strain rates reduce dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Reduced dislocation mobility promotes the onset of deformation twinning.
Deformation twinning increases strength through enhanced strain hardening.
The twinning-associated increase in strength occurs at the expense of ductility.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, thermal activation enables easier dislocation motion and glide-dominated plasticity.
Lower temperature or higher strain rate produces dislocation pile-ups.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate testing will produce higher yield strength and ultimate strength than the room-temperature, moderate-rate baseline.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate testing will produce lower ductility than the baseline.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation will produce significantly more deformation twins than room-temperature, moderate-rate deformation.
Twin density and dislocation-slip features can be used as the structural mediator connecting temperature and strain rate to mechanical response.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase, defect-minimized, solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Significant secondary phases or cast defects may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Outside the tested temperature and strain-rate regime, mechanisms such as dynamic recrystallization may dominate.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in deformation twinning under low-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions would falsify the proposed glide-to-twinning mechanism.
